newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt regulates closing prices on bourse.
newsitem.headline: Egypt regulates closing prices on bourse.

text.p: Egypt took another step on Wednesday to reform its financial sector with a new rule aimed to prevent investors from manipulating prices on the emerging stock market.
The new economy minister, Youssef Boutros-Ghali, signed the decree changing the way closing stock prices are calculated and announced, a statement from his office said.
"Some people were using the shares to manipulate the market and to get the prices up towards the very end of the day," Mahmoud Mohiedin, the minister's economic adviser, told Reuters.
"This will use a weighted average of a share price during the day and eliminate transactions of less than 100 shares."
Egypt has embarked in earnest on reforms since early 1996 and is updating investment laws and privatising, much of it through the country's bourse.

The decree, which the statement said was part of "ongoing capital market reforms", said: "Prices will be calculated using a weighted average price - based on a number of shares, for a volume no less than one hundred shares."

The decree, effective August 10, says operational prices and other offers should be announced on the bourse. "The closing price of a security shall be invalidated if the security remains inoperative for three successive months. If another three consecutive months elapse, the security will be cancelled from the listing of the stock exchange," the decree says.
New Egyptian bourse Chairman Sherif Raafat told Reuters in July that his immediate aim was to increase market transparency and update bourse infrastructure to make investing easier.
Brokers say transactions take days to process. Timely corporate information is not readily available and the few trading rules are not strictly enforced.
This month the bourse received a new trading system but its immediate effect was to slow down trade as brokers adapt.
Analysts say that the move is a sign of a young market and comes at a time when Egypt is trying to modernise the bourse.

Mohammad Maher, analyst at Prime Securities, said that the new technique of dividing the value of the traded shares by the day's volume aimed to eliminate what he called "fictitious" or "artificial" transactions at the end of the trading day by investors hoping to influence closing prices.

"The international markets use the last trading price as a closing price. There is a big difference between us and them," he said. "This is so nobody can manipulate the rates of trading. It's like a transitional decision until the market becomes more educated and behaves in a more professional way."
Long term goals include weaning the bourse from state share offerings and making it a forum where private firms raise capital, and to channel direct foreign investment into Egypt.

"Egypt's still-small but rapidly growing 60.3 billion pound ($17.8 billion) stock market is attracting numerous domestic and foreign investors," said the U.S. embassy July economic report. It said about 60 of the 700 firms listed are actively traded.
The Capital Market Authority overall index has lost some momentum and is now languishing at levels last seen in January.
